2027-06-22.title: Sixth Tuesday of the Apostles · Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, Martyrs
2027-06-22.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: We have a house eternal in the heavens

2027-06-22.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. The First Set calendar lists Sts John Fisher and Thomas More (the calendar prints “Moore”) with the proper readings given above, besides the readings of the Sixth Tuesday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar they are an optional memorial today, together with St Paulinus of Nola. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-06-22.verse: Yet if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace, but glorify God because you bear this name.
theo: Saint Paul knew about tents. Luke tells us that in Corinth he lodged with Aquila and Priscilla, “and they worked together, by trade they were tentmakers” (Acts 18:3). So when he writes to the same Corinthians about death and eternal life, he reaches for the image he knew best: “For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.” A tent is good, but it is temporary; it is pitched for a journey and folded at the end. Our bodies are such tents. They grow tired, they are wounded, and one day they are taken down. Paul does not despise the tent; he groans in it, “longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling”, not to be stripped bare but to be “further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.” This is the Christian hope: not escape from the body but its transformation in the resurrection. And the pledge of it is already given: “He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.” The Greek word means a first instalment, the advance payment that promises the rest. The Spirit poured out at Pentecost is God's down payment on our eternal home. Therefore, says Paul, “we are always confident… for we walk by faith, not by sight.”

The Gospel turns to a lamp. “Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket, or under the bed, and not on the lampstand?” Every Kerala home once had its nilavilakku, lit at dusk, set high in the front room so that its light would reach every corner. No one lights a lamp to hide it. The faith given to us at baptism, when a lighted candle was placed in our parents' hands, is not meant to be hidden under the bed of private feeling. “For there is nothing hidden, except to be disclosed; nor is anything secret, except to come to light.” Jesus adds a warning about how we listen: “Pay attention to what you hear; the measure you give will be the measure you get, and still more will be given you.” Those who give themselves generously to the word receive more light; those who hold back find even the little they have growing dim.

Today the First Set calendar honours two men who would not put their lamp under a basket, though it cost them their lives: St John Fisher and St Thomas More, martyrs of England in 1535. When King Henry VIII broke with Rome and had himself declared Supreme Head of the Church in England, the oath that was demanded of his subjects touched both his second marriage and the authority of the Pope. John Fisher, Bishop of Rochester, a learned and austere pastor, refused it; he was the only bishop of England to stand firm. While he lay in the Tower of London, Pope Paul III named him a cardinal. He was beheaded on 22 June 1535. It is told that on the way to execution he opened his New Testament and his eyes fell on the words, “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Thomas More was a layman: a lawyer, a scholar, a loving husband and father, the friend of the king and once his Lord Chancellor, famous for his wit and for his book Utopia. He did not seek martyrdom. For more than a year in the Tower he kept silent and used every honest means the law allowed. But he would not swear against his conscience, and he was condemned for treason on false testimony and beheaded on 6 July 1535, declaring, according to the reports of the time, that he died the king's good servant, but God's first. Pope Pius XI canonised them together in 1935, and in 2000 St John Paul II named Thomas More patron of statesmen and politicians.

The readings of their commemoration describe their road. Peter writes to Christians facing hostility: “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that is taking place among you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you are sharing Christ’s sufferings”. He draws a sharp line: let none of you suffer as a criminal, “Yet if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace, but glorify God because you bear this name.” Fisher and More were not rebels; they honoured the king in everything that was the king's. They suffered only for the name. And Jesus had warned the Twelve: “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves… you will be dragged before governors and kings because of me”. More was wise as a serpent in his careful silence and innocent as a dove in his refusal to lie. Both found that the promise held: “what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” In our own time, Christians in many lands, and in some places in our own country, pay a price for their faith; Christians in public life in India face daily pressures to bend their conscience. Today's martyrs remind them, and us, that a well-formed conscience is a lamp that must not be hidden, and that the earthly tent may be taken down, but the house from God is eternal. “The one who endures to the end will be saved.”
outline: A tentmaker writes about tents; two martyrs who did not hide their lamp.
Point 1 · A house not made with hands
The tent of the body, the groan of hope, the Spirit as guarantee.
Point 2 · The lamp on the lampstand
Faith is not hidden; the measure we give.
Point 3 · The king's good servant, but God's first
Fisher and More: conscience, courage and the Spirit who speaks.
“If any of you suffers as a Christian… glorify God because you bear this name.”
live: When fear of illness or death troubles you today, pray: “Lord, you have given me the Spirit as a guarantee.”
Put the lamp on the lampstand (Mark 4:21)
Do not hide your faith this week: make the sign of the cross before a meal in public, or speak up kindly for what is right at work or school.
fathers: I am writing to all the Churches that I die willingly for God, unless you hinder me. Let me be food for the wild beasts, through whom I may reach God. I am the wheat of God, and I am ground by the teeth of the beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ.
Your cruelty does not succeed. It is rather an attraction to our religion. The more you mow us down, the more we grow: the blood of Christians is seed.
magis: Martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith: it means bearing witness even unto death. The martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity.

The citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the demands of the moral order, to the fundamental rights of persons or the teachings of the Gospel: “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29).

Deep within his conscience man discovers a law which he has not laid upon himself but which he must obey; conscience is man's most secret core and sanctuary, where he is alone with God, whose voice echoes in his depths.
saints: Sts John Fisher (1469–1535), Bishop of Rochester and cardinal, and Thomas More (1478–1535), layman, husband and father, Lord Chancellor of England, martyrs, canonised together in 1935; St Thomas More is patron of statesmen and politicians (First Set calendar, with proper readings). In the Latin calendar also St Paulinus of Nola (about 354–431), bishop, who gave away his wealth and served the poor.

19–24 June: the end of the fifth week and the sixth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs, are listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings; in the Latin calendar, St Romuald. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 21: St Aloysius Gonzaga is listed without proper readings (in the Latin calendar an obligatory memorial). Tue 22: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs, with proper readings. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist. Then Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season; Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation.
2027-06-22.prayer: Lord God, you have given us the Holy Spirit as the guarantee of an eternal home not made with hands. While we live in this tent of the body, teach us to walk by faith and not by sight. Lord Jesus, you sent your apostles like sheep among wolves and promised them your Spirit when they stood before governors and kings: as you gave St John Fisher and St Thomas More the courage to keep faith and conscience even unto death, give us the grace to set our lamp on the lampstand, to serve our country faithfully and you above all. Strengthen those who suffer for your name today, and bring us all to the house of the Father. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: Every Holy Qurbana is offered in communion with the martyrs, who gave their bodies as Christ gave his. The Body we receive is the pledge of the house not made with hands; nourished by it, the martyrs walked to the scaffold, and we walk by faith through our own trials.

quick: Paul: if the earthly tent is destroyed, we have a house from God; the Spirit is the guarantee; we walk by faith, not by sight.
Jesus: a lamp is not put under a basket but on the lampstand; the measure you give will be the measure you get.
Sts John Fisher and Thomas More died in 1535 rather than betray conscience and the unity of the Church: the king's good servant, but God's first.
2027-06-22.action: Do one thing today that lets your faith be seen, gently and without fear.
2027-06-22.question: Where am I tempted to hide my lamp under a basket?
kidsaint: Thomas More was a clever lawyer in England who loved his wife and children very much and made everyone laugh. He became the most important helper of the king. But one day the king asked him to make a promise that was against his conscience and against the Church. Thomas said no. He was put in prison and then put to death. He said he was the king's good servant, but God's first. Lesson: love your country and obey good rules, but always put God first!
term: The Syriac word for a martyr, from the root meaning ‘to bear witness’, like the Greek martys. Our tradition calls St George ‘Geevarghese Sahada’, the martyr. A martyr is first of all a witness, one whose life and death speak of Christ. Malayalam: സഹദാ, രക്തസാക്ഷി.

family.explain: Jesus asks: would you light a lamp and then hide it under a basket or under the bed? No! You put it up high so everyone can see. Our faith is like that lamp. Today we remember two brave men from England, a bishop called John Fisher and a father called Thomas More. A king wanted them to say something they knew was wrong. They said no, even though they were put to death. They let their light shine.
family.intention: We pray for Christians who suffer for their faith, and for leaders and politicians, that they may follow their conscience.
family.ask: Ask: “How can our family let the light of Jesus shine this week?”

illus: A young Catholic officer in a government department in Kerala was asked by his superior to sign a report approving a building that did not meet the safety rules. ‘Everyone signs,’ he was told. ‘It is only a formality.’ He took the file home and did not sleep. In the morning, before going to the office, he went to the weekday Qurbana, and the reading was about the lamp that must not be put under a basket. He returned the file unsigned, with a short, polite note giving the reasons. For months he was passed over and given the dullest work. Two years later, during the monsoon, part of a similar building in another district collapsed. An inquiry was opened, and his note was found in the file. ‘I did not feel brave,’ he said later. ‘I only remembered that my conscience is where I meet God, and that he would see the file too.’

pm.open: Holy Spirit, guarantee of our eternal home, come upon us now. Give us the courage of the apostles and the martyrs, that we may not hide the lamp of our faith. Amen.
share: If the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God (2 Corinthians 5:1). How do I think about my own death?
For we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). Where is God asking me to trust without seeing?
Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket? (Mark 4:21). Where do I hide my faith?
Yet if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace (1 Peter 4:16). What has my faith cost me, and what am I willing to give?
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that she may proclaim the Gospel with courage before every authority.
For Christians who are persecuted, imprisoned or threatened for their faith, that the Spirit may speak through them.
For politicians, judges, officials and all in public life, that through the prayers of St Thomas More they may serve the common good with honest consciences.
For bishops, that like St John Fisher they may be faithful shepherds who defend the truth.
For the dying, that they may pass from the earthly tent to the house not made with hands.
pm.close: Father, your martyrs John and Thomas served you above all and endured to the end. Make us lamps on the lampstand, faithful in small things and in great, until we come to our eternal home. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul was a tentmaker, and he tells us that our body is like a tent: good, but not permanent. “For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).
God has already given us the Holy Spirit as a guarantee, like an advance payment, that we will have that eternal house. So we are confident, and we walk by faith, not by sight.
Jesus says that no one lights a lamp to hide it under a basket. Our faith is a lamp. It is meant to be seen, in our homes, at our work, in our words and choices.

Today we remember two men who did not hide their lamp: St John Fisher, a bishop, and St Thomas More, a husband, father and lawyer. When King Henry VIII demanded an oath against their conscience and against the unity of the Church, they refused. Both were beheaded in 1535. Thomas More said he died the king's good servant, but God's first.

Saint Peter says: if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God because you bear this name. May we love our country and serve it well, but put God first. And when our earthly tent is folded, may we find the house that God has prepared for us. Amen.
kids: Children, would you hide a lamp under your bed? No! Jesus says our faith is like a lamp. Today we remember St Thomas More, a father who loved to laugh, and St John Fisher, a bishop. They chose God first, even when the king was angry. Let your light shine today by being honest and kind!

intro: Theme: “Yet if any of you suffers as a Christian, do not consider it a disgrace, but glorify God because you bear this name.”
The tent of the body and the house from God, the lamp on the lampstand, and two martyrs who served their king but God first.

For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
points.apply: Visit or call someone who is seriously ill this week, and pray with them for the hope of the resurrection.

sub: Nothing hidden that will not come to light.
q: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
He said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under the bushel basket, or under the bed, and not on the lampstand?
points.apply: Let your faith be seen in one concrete act at work, school or in public this week.

points.h: The king's good servant, but God's first
sub: The Spirit who speaks before governors and kings.
q: But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods and we will not worship the golden statue that you have set up.
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than any human authority.
points.apply: Examine where you are pressed to act against conscience, and ask St Thomas More for courage to say no with kindness.

concl: Our body is a tent, but God has given us his Spirit as a pledge of an eternal house.
Like Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, let us set our lamp on the lampstand, serve our country well and God first.
2027-06-22.resolve: This week, pray for the dying and the persecuted, let your faith be seen in one act, and refuse one thing that goes against your conscience.
